title: Why Óbidos tastes the way it does

lede.text: Óbidos is a town ringed by a 14th-century wall, at the end of a run of hills and knolls from the Serra de Montejunto. Together with loam to clay soils of brown and red limestone, they give fresh whites and fruity reds.

chapters.title: A patchwork of hills running to a walled town
paras: From the slopes of the Serra de Montejunto, towards the northwest and as far as Óbidos, a long run of colinas and outeiros (hills and knolls) is covered by a "manta de retalhos", a patchwork quilt in which the vine stands out.

Óbidos itself is surrounded by a wall from the 14th century that still keeps its medieval identity. It is the ex-libris, the emblem, of an important farming region where the vine has always held a leading place.
The denomination covers parts of four municipalities: Bombarral, Cadaval, Caldas da Rainha and Óbidos. It lies in the Oeste, the west of Portugal.

fly.label: Óbidos and its wall
fly.caption: The town inside its 14th-century wall, the emblem of a farming region where the vine has always held a leading place.

fly.label: Serra de Montejunto
fly.caption: The hills and knolls of Óbidos start on the slopes of this range and run northwest.

chapters.title: Loam to clay over brown and red limestone
paras: The soils have a loam to clay texture, of brown and red limestone.
Vineyards must sit on brown or red limestone soils, or on brown or red Mediterranean soils made from non-limestone material. They also need an exposure that suits quality wine.

chapters.title: Fresh whites and bottle-fermented bubbles
paras: Óbidos makes still wines and white sparkling wine. 39 grape varieties are allowed, white and red.
From these hills and soils come reds that are open in colour with ruby tones. They are fruity and soft, with some body.
Whites are smooth and very fresh. They are bright, with fruity and floral aromas and light mineral touches.

Sparkling whites have a fine, lasting foam and a fine, fruity aroma in which the secondary aromas stand out. They show good complexity and a good balance between acidity and freshness. They are made by the classic method of fermentation in the bottle.

White wines come from white grapes, or from red grapes run off the skins by "bica aberta". Rosados use the same run-off with a very light maceration of red grapes. Reds come only from red grapes, with intensive maceration.
Reds must reach at least 12% alcohol. Whites, rosados and sparkling wines need at least 11%. Yields are capped at 70 hl per hectare for red and 90 hl for white, rosado and sparkling.
Vines must be at least four years past grafting and trained low, as a bush (taça) or on a cordon.
